content.text: Charged by the Vanar army to find Sita, held captive across the sea in Ravana's Lanka, Hanuman alone resolved to make the leap no other could attempt. Standing on the mountain's height before his kinsmen, he vowed: 'Swift as a shaft from Rama's bow to Ravan's city will I go, and if she be not there will fly and seek the lady in the sky; or, if in heaven she be not found, will hither bring the giant bound.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

content.text: Hanuman sprang from the mountain crest across the ocean toward Lanka, his shadow flying over the sea 'like a ship before the gale.' The mountain Mainaka, moved by gratitude to Rama's line, rose from the sea to offer him rest — but Hanuman, single-minded in his mission, would not pause: 'I may not rest, the Vanar cried; I must not stay or turn aside. Yet pleased am I, thou noblest hill, and as the deed accept thy will.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

content.text: The serpent-mother Surasa barred his path in monstrous form, declaring him her destined prey by Brahma's decree, and opened her jaws impossibly wide to swallow him. Hanuman matched her, growing his own form ever larger, then in an instant shrank himself smaller than a thumb, darted through her mouth, and emerged unharmed on the other side — defeating her by wit rather than force, and she blessed his onward journey.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

content.text: Next the demoness Sinhika seized his shadow from the deep and opened her jaws to devour him. Hanuman shrank his body, leapt inside her gaping mouth, tore through her from within, and burst out again 'with thought-like speed,' slaying her outright — a feat the watching spirits hailed from the sky: 'Well hast thou fought a wondrous fight... Ne're can they fail in whom combine such valour, thought, and skill as thine.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

content.text: Having reduced himself to the size of a cat to search unseen, Hanuman entered Ravana's pleasure gardens and at last found the Ashoka grove, reasoning that a grieving queen would be drawn to its cool, lovely shade: 'Here the sad queen will roam apart, and dream of Rama in her heart' — the quiet, careful searching of a devoted servant, patient even after crossing an ocean and battling monsters to get there.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

content.text: Hanuman's entire mission across this batch's chunks illustrates a single, sustained quality: total devotion to Rama's purpose that neither honour (Mainaka's offered rest), nor threat (Surasa), nor mortal danger (Sinhika) could turn aside from its object — reasoning always by resourcefulness rather than force alone when force would not serve.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

content.text: Hanuman's leap across the ocean to Lanka, and his subsequent discovery of Sita in the Ashoka grove, is the turning point of the Ramayana's Sundara Kanda (Book V) — the moment that confirms Sita is alive and locatable, and sets in motion the war that will free her. Tradition venerates Hanuman above all as the ideal of selfless, resourceful service (dasya bhakti) to Rama.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V
